paragraphs.text: BY THE SAME GREGORY: TO THE GREEKS, FROM COMMON NOTIONS. If the name "God" indicated persons, then in speaking of three persons we would necessarily speak of three gods. But if the name "God" signifies essence, then, since we confess one essence of the Holy Trinity, we rightly glorify one God, because "God" is the one name of the one essence. So, in keeping with both the essence and the name, God is one, not three. For we do not say "God and God and God" in the way we say "Father and Son and Holy Spirit". With the names that signify the persons we join the conjunction "and", because the persons are not the same. They are rather distinct, and they differ from one another as the meanings of the names differ. But to the name "God", which indicates the essence on the basis of some property belonging to it, we do not attach the conjunction "and" so as to say "God and God and God". For the essence of which the persons are is the same, and it is this that the name "God" signifies, so God too is the same. And the same thing is never joined by "and" to a further designation of itself. When we say "the Father God, and the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God", or "God the Father, and God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit", the "and" that we join is, in its sense, joined to the names of the persons. For instance: to the Father, to the Son, to the Holy Spirit. It is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, that is, person and person and person, and that is why there are three persons. But the name "God" is predicated absolutely, and in the same way, of each of the persons, without the conjunction "and". So we cannot say "God and God and God". We must understand that the name is uttered three times because of the persons that underlie it, but that in being repeated a second and a third time it is put forward without the conjunction "and", because there is not one God and then another God. For it is not insofar as the Father keeps his distinctness from the Son that the Father is God. Otherwise the Son would not be God: if the Father were God because he is Father, then, since the Son is not Father, the Son would not be God. But if the Son is God, he is not God because he is Son. Likewise the Father is not God because he is Father, but because of the kind of essence that belongs to the Father, and to the Son as well, he is

God. And it is for this reason that the Father is God, and the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God. Since the essence is not divided in each of the persons so as to make three essences corresponding to the persons, it is clear that the name which signifies the essence will not be divided either, nor will "God" be divided so as to make three gods. Just as the Father is essence, the Son essence and the Holy Spirit essence, and yet there are not three essences, so too the Father is God, the Son God and the Holy Spirit God, and yet there are not three gods. For God is one and the same, since the essence too is one and the same, even though each of the persons is said to be both possessed of essence and God. Otherwise we would have to speak of three essences, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, since each of the persons is essence, and that is absurd. For we do not call Peter and Paul and Barnabas three essences either. Rather, since we speak of one single essence, to which the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit belong, we consistently speak of one God, even though we believe that each of the persons is both possessed of essence and God. Because the Father differs from the Son and from the Holy Spirit, we speak of three persons. In the same way, since they do not differ in essence, and the persons are identical with respect to it, they will certainly be identical with respect to the name "God" as well. For this name indicates the essence. It does not present what the essence is, since that is incomprehensible; it is taken from some property belonging to the essence and points to it indirectly. It is a property of the eternal essence, to which the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit belong, to oversee, behold and know all things, even hidden things. The name "God" is taken from this, and in its proper sense it signifies that essence. Since, then, this essence is one, and the name that points to it (I mean "God") is one, God will properly be one, in keeping with the account of the essence. For "God" indicates not a person but the essence. If "God" indicated a person, only one of the persons would be called God, namely the one signified by that name, just as only the Father is called Father, because this name indicates a person. Someone might say that we call Peter and Paul and Barnabas three essences, meaning partial essences, that is, [?] (for this is the most proper way to put it). Let him know that when we speak of a partial or particular essence we mean nothing other than an individual, which is a person. And "God" does not follow upon persons, as has been shown. What, then, must be said to the objection that we call Peter and Paul and Barnabas three men? We do not do so because they are these persons, for persons are not signified by the name that signifies the common essence. Nor is the so-called partial or particular essence the same thing as the person. Why, then, do we speak of three men, when they are of one essence, the essence that "man" indicates? If we speak this way [?] neither because of the persons nor because of the phrase "partial" or "particular essence", then our answer is this: we say it by an improper use of language and not properly, because of a custom that has prevailed for necessary reasons,

reasons that are not found in the Holy Trinity. They are as follows. The definition of man is not always found in the same individuals or persons. When earlier ones die, others take their place; and again, while the same ones often remain, others are added. So it is found sometimes in these and sometimes in those, sometimes in more and sometimes in fewer. Because individuals, in whom the definition of man is found, are taken away, die and are born, we are compelled to speak of many men and of few. Common usage has been knocked off course by the change and alteration of the persons, even contrary to the very account of the essence, so that in a way we count essences along with the persons. But nothing of this kind ever happens in the Holy Trinity, because the persons spoken of are always the same, not one set and then another, and they remain in the same state and in the same way. The Trinity receives no addition that would make it a group of four, and no diminution that would make it a pair. No one is begotten of the Father, or proceeds from him or from one of the persons, in such a way that the Trinity might at some point become four. Nor does any of these three persons ever die, so that the Trinity might become two. Since no addition or diminution, no change or alteration, ever happens to the three persons, it is absurd to speak of three gods in addition to the three persons. Again, the human persons do not all have their being directly from the same person. Some come from this one and others from that one, so that, besides the many things caused, the causes too are many and different. But in the Holy Trinity it is not so. It is one and the same person of the Father from whom the Son is begotten and the Holy Spirit proceeds. Therefore we properly say that the one who is the single cause of those he causes is one God, since he also coexists with them. For the persons of the Godhead are not divided from one another by time or by place, nor by will, pursuit, activity or any affection of the kind found among human beings. They are distinguished only in that the Father is Father and not Son, the Son is Son and not Father, and likewise the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son. So no necessity compels us to call the three persons three gods, in the way that among ourselves we call the many persons many men, for the reasons given. We do not do so by any necessity of reason, since the same thing cannot be both one and many in the same respect. Peter and Paul and Barnabas, in respect of "man", are one man, and in that same respect, in respect of "man", they cannot be many. They are called many men by an improper use of language and not properly, and sensible people would not prefer an improper expression to a proper one. Therefore it must not be said of the three persons of the divine essence that they are three gods in respect of "God". God is one and the same, because the essence that "God" signifies is identical, as we have said.

Someone may ask: "Then how does Scripture count 'three men' [?]?" Let him observe this. Scripture gives us the Son and the Holy Spirit, and God the Word, and God who is not the Word, that is, God the Father and God the Holy Spirit. Yet in handing down "God" it refuses altogether to speak of three gods, for it regards polytheism as impiety. It proclaims one God throughout, neither confusing the persons nor dividing the Godhead, but rather preserving the identity of the Godhead in the distinctive properties of the hypostases, that is, of three persons. If the one who says such things wants to learn the truth, let him know that Scripture says "three" even though it knows all men as one man, as in the saying, "Man, his days are like grass." Like a good nurse, it treats human beings as its own infants. At times it lisps along with them and, like them, uses some of their words, without losing sight of what is perfect. The same Scripture says that God has ears and eyes and the other parts of a body, but it does not hand this down as doctrine, as though defining the Divine as composite. In the manner just described, it sets forth its doctrines by transferring terms from our own world, in order to lift up those who cannot go straight to incorporeal things. It says that God is Spirit, and teaches us that wherever one goes he is present, simple and uncircumscribed. So too it says "three men" out of custom, so that what is common and in use among the many may not seem strange. And it says "one" for the sake of accuracy, so as not to unsettle the goal, which is also found in the nature of things. The first we regard as a condescension made for the use and benefit of the more childlike; the second we define as doctrine, set forth to confirm and hand down perfection. But again, some argue as follows. We say that hypostasis does not differ from hypostasis insofar as it is hypostasis, and yet all hypostases are not on that account one hypostasis. Essence does not differ from essence, and yet all essences are not on that account one essence. In the same way, they say, we might say that God does not differ from God, and yet the three hypostases of which "God" is predicated are not on that account one God. And again, when we say that man does not differ from man, we do not deny that Peter and Paul and Barnabas are three men. For essence differs from essence, not insofar as it is essence but insofar as it is such-and-such an essence; hypostasis differs from hypostasis insofar as it is such-and-such a hypostasis; and man differs from man as such-and-such a man. So again God differs from God as such-and-such a God; and "such" and "such" are customarily said of two or more. That is their argument. We, however, shall show that the whole thing is a sophism, using their own statements. We shall show that one must not say "such-and-such a God and such-and-such a God", or "such-and-such a man and such-and-such a man", but rather "such-and-such a hypostasis of God" and "such-and-such a hypostasis of man". For we rightly speak of many hypostases of the one man and of three hypostases of the one God. When "such" is used, it serves to distinguish one thing from another that shares with it in the name to which "such" is added. For example, we call man "such-and-such an animal" because we want to distinguish him from the horse,

for instance, which shares with him in the name "animal" but differs from him as irrational differs from rational. One thing is distinguished from another by essence, or by hypostasis, or by both essence and hypostasis. By essence, man is distinguished from horse; by hypostasis, Paul from Peter; by essence and hypostasis, this hypostasis of man from that hypostasis of horse. Once the account has been made clear of things that differ simply in essence, and of things that differ in hypostasis and not in essence, the account of things distinguished in essence [and hypostasis?] will also be plain. Both they and we agree that things differing in essence are called two or three essences, and that things differing in hypostasis are likewise called two or three hypostases. Where we disagree is this: they say that in the case of Peter and Paul one must speak of "men", while we say that this is not proper and not in keeping with scientific reasoning. For common and improper usage counts for nothing in this argument, since it has no force either to refute anything or to establish it. So let it first be made clear to us why we say that man and horse, or horse and dog, differ as such-and-such an essence. Is it not plain that they differ from one another in the features that usually separate essences, such as rational and irrational, neighing, barking and the like? For when we say "such-and-such an essence", we mean nothing other than an existence that shares in life, as opposed to one that does not; or an existence naturally able to reason, as distinguished from one marked by irrationality; or an existence characterized by neighing; and so on. In place of such differences and properties, "such" is placed before the essence, or before any genus, to distinguish the species under it: "such" or "such-and-such an animal" stands for "rational" or "irrational". And again, we say that Peter differs from Paul insofar as each of them is such-and-such a hypostasis, since they differ from one another in some of the features that naturally make up a hypostasis and not an essence, such as baldness, tallness, fatherhood, sonship and the like. For it is plain that species and individual are not the same, that is, essence and hypostasis are not the same. The word "hypostasis" at once leads the hearer's mind to look for a scar, grey eyes, a father, a son, or something similar. By species I mean essence, that is, what lets us know a rational, mortal animal capable of mind and knowledge, or a non-rational, mortal, neighing animal, and so forth. If essence and individual (which is hypostasis) are not the same, then the features that characterize the one and the other are not the same either. And if these are not the same, they cannot be joined to the same names: the one set belongs with the names that pertain to essence or are applied to essence, the other with the names said of the individual.

There are, then, three names under inquiry: essence, individual and man. To essence we attach and yoke "such", in order to distinguish, as I said, the species under it that differ from one another in essence. To hypostasis we likewise yoke "such", in order to distinguish persons that share with one another in this name, that is, "hypostasis", and that differ from one another not by what characterizes essence but by what are called accidents. In which way, then, do they want to join "such" to the name "man"? For disputed matters find their solution in what is commonly agreed. As applied to essence? Then the things under it would be distinguished from one another by an essential difference, which is not the case, for Paul does not differ in essence from Peter, and "man" is predicated of both. As applied to the hypostasis of a person? Then "man" would not indicate essence, which it is absurd to say. For "man" signifies what is common to the essence, not a particular person, such as Paul or Barnabas. So by scientific reasoning, at least, "such" cannot attach to "man" in any way. If common usage is at a loss here, and improperly uses the names of essence to indicate persons, that has nothing to do with the exact rule of logical science. But why do I attack customary misuse, which is at a loss in such matters, forgetting that we ourselves often lack proper terms and misuse other, improper names to convey what we mean? Still, let this be clear to us: if in the case of Peter and Paul we could say, "Man does not differ from man insofar as he is man, but insofar as he is such-and-such a man", then we could also say of them, "Essence does not differ from essence insofar as it is essence, but insofar as it is such-and-such an essence." But if this cannot be said, because Peter and Paul have the same essence, then the other cannot be said either, since the name "man" indicates essence. And if it is not consistent to join "such" and "such" to the name "man", then neither do we properly speak of two or three men. If this has been shown in the case of man, how much more fitting it will be, in the case of the eternal and divine essence, that none of the hypostases be called "such-and-such a God" and "such-and-such a God"; that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit not be spoken of as "God and God and God"; and that three gods not be taught as doctrine, even in thought. It has therefore been established by the argument, in a way that is just, consistent and scientific on our part, that we speak of one God, the creator of all things, even though he is contemplated in three persons or hypostases: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
